summary: Defines a protocol that lets a device ask a server in its local access network where it is. The request and response travel over HTTP or HTTP over TLS, and the answer can be location information itself or a reference to it. It is designed to be extensible and independent of the way the network is built.

eli5.summary: Your phone asks the network, "where am I?" over the same kind of messages web pages use. The network answers with your spot, or with a note saying where you can look it up.

questions: how does a device ask the network for its location
how does a device get its location from the network
what is a location information server
subtitle: How a device asks the network it is plugged into where it is, using plain HTTP and XML.

tldr.problem: Many devices cannot work out their own location, and even those that can may do it faster with help. The access network usually knows better, but there was no standard way to ask it.
tldr.mechanism: The device discovers a Location Information Server (LIS) and sends it an XML locationRequest in an HTTP POST. The LIS identifies the device by its source IP address and replies with a locationResponse holding the location itself (by value), Location URIs (by reference), or an error.
tldr.outcome: HELD is a Standards Track protocol that supports both forms of location and requires HTTP over TLS support. It is updated by RFC 7840.

facts.label: Location URI expiry
facts.value: Not over 24 hours, at least 30 minutes

facts.label: Device identifier
facts.value: Source IP address of the request

today: RFC 5985 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 7840. It has not been obsoleted, so it remains the base HELD specification, with the changes in RFC 7840 applied on top.

sections.title: Asking the Access Network for Location
sections.content:
RFC 5985 defines HTTP-Enabled Location Delivery (HELD), a Layer 7 Location Configuration Protocol. A Device uses it to retrieve its location from a Location Information Server (LIS) inside its access network, which can be wired (for example DSL or cable) or wireless (for example WiMAX).

The LIS exists because not every Device can determine its own location, and even a Device that can may find it more efficient with assistance. The RFC does not say how the LIS works out the location. It only defines the conversation between the Device and the LIS.

Two forms of location can be retrieved. Location by value returns a literal location object. Location by reference returns a Location URI that the Device can pass on instead. A LIS can offer both at the same time.
sections.eli5: Some gadgets do not know where they are, like someone asleep in the back of a car. The network knows, so the gadget just asks it.

sections.title: How a Request Finds the Right Place
sections.content:
Before anything else, the Device MUST discover the URI of its LIS. Discovery itself is out of scope and is specified in RFC 5986. The URI SHOULD come from an authorized and authenticated entity, and an HTTPS URI is RECOMMENDED.

The LIS needs some way to know which Device is asking. In this RFC the identifier is the IP address of the Device, taken from the source address of the location request. Other identifiers are possible but out of scope.

That choice has limits. If a NAT, a VPN or another form of address change sits between the Device and the LIS, the location returned could be wrong. A residential NAT is typically fine because the area covered is small. A VPN for a teleworker, or an enterprise NAT covering a large area, may not be. In those cases the LIS should return an error if it cannot determine the location, and Devices that will connect to VPN, SOCKS or HTTP proxy servers should perform discovery and a first HELD query before making those connections.

HELD attributes location to a Device, not to a person. The RFC argues the Device needs the same privacy protection a user would demand.
sections.eli5: The network works out who is asking by looking at the return address on the envelope. If the envelope was relayed through someone else, the answer might be about the wrong place.

sections.title: Requests, Responses and Errors
sections.content:
HELD defines three messages, all XML documents encoded in UTF-8: locationRequest, locationResponse and error. They use the media type application/held+xml, and the charset parameter MUST be included.

A request can carry a responseTime attribute, a hint in milliseconds for how long the Device will wait, or one of the purposes emergencyRouting and emergencyDispatch. The LIS is not obliged to follow the time strictly. A request can also carry a locationType element listing any, geodetic, civic or locationURI. If it is absent, any is assumed. The LIS MUST ignore any part of a request it does not understand, except the document element.

A successful response MUST contain a location object (a PIDF-LO document) and/or Location URIs. The LIS MUST NOT include any means of identifying the Device in the PIDF-LO unless it can verify the identifier and a Rule Maker expressly permits it.

An error message MUST have a code attribute and MAY have message elements with human-readable diagnostics, in any language marked with xml:lang.
sections.eli5: There are only three kinds of note: a question, an answer and an "I could not do that". Each one is written in a tidy, standard form so that any computer can read it.

sections.title: Location Types, Exactness and Location URIs
sections.content:
The exact attribute on locationType controls how strict the LIS must be. With the default false, the LIS SHOULD return the requested types but MAY add others or substitute alternatives. This allows soft failover: a notebook that prefers a civic address can still get a geodetic one from a wireless modem. With true, the LIS MUST return only the requested types or an error. The protocol cannot ask for just one of a subset of types.

A locationUriSet in a response MUST have an expires attribute. It is RECOMMENDED not to exceed 24 hours and SHOULD be a minimum of 30 minutes. It limits how long the URIs stay valid, not how long a location stays valid. All times MUST be in UTC.

Each Location URI is unique to the requesting Device and SHOULD NOT contain information that identifies the Device or Target. The Device cannot set or learn the access policy for a URI, so it SHOULD protect the URI like a location object: send it over encrypted channels and only to authorized parties. How a URI is dereferenced is out of scope (see RFC 5808).
sections.eli5: You can say "give me exactly a street address, or nothing", or you can say "a street address would be nice, but anything helpful is fine". A Location URI is like a claim ticket that someone else can use to ask where you are, and it stops working after a while.

sections.title: The HTTP Binding
sections.content:
A conforming LIS and Device MUST support both HTTP and HTTP over TLS. HELD uses only a strict subset of HTTP, so a LIS is not a fully compliant HTTP server. A HELD request travels in the body of an HTTP POST, and POST is the only method required. The Device MUST include a Host header, and both sides MUST use application/held+xml in the Content-Type and Accept headers.

HELD errors are application-level, so an error message MUST be carried by a 200 OK response, and the HTTP status for any locationResponse or error MUST be in the 2xx series. The LIS SHOULD set cache control to disable caching of location objects and Location URIs by intermediaries. Devices MUST NOT use the Expect or Range headers.

Because Device and LIS may have no prior relationship, the LIS SHOULD NOT require the Device to authenticate. Denying access could block services such as emergency calling. Over TLS, the Device MUST authenticate the server using the method in RFC 2818, with a wildcard allowed only as the whole leftmost label, and SHOULD fail the request if authentication fails, except in an emergency.
sections.eli5: HELD rides on the same delivery trucks as web pages, but it only uses the simplest truck features. The truck must be able to lock its doors (TLS) so nobody peeks at the package.

sections.title: Accuracy, Privacy and Spoofing
sections.content:
The RFC names two risks: the client receives incorrect location information, or an unauthorized entity receives location information. TLS gives the client a way to authenticate the LIS and protects responses from modification and eavesdropping. Without TLS, in most cases the response is neither protected from modification nor hidden from observers on the path.

The LIS MUST verify that the client is the target of the returned location and MUST NOT provide location to other entities. By default the only client check is IP return routability: the response goes to the source address. That is vulnerable to IP address spoofing, and a re-used address could let a new Device receive the old Device's location.

The limits on this are that Location URIs MUST have a limited lifetime, and that the LIS and network SHOULD be set up so the LIS notices Device movement and address changes. If the LIS can no longer determine a Device's location, all Location URIs for that Device SHOULD be invalidated.
sections.eli5: Because the network answers whoever is at your address, someone who borrows or steals your address could get your answer. So the claim tickets expire, and the network cancels them if it loses track of you.

messages.label: locationRequest (HTTP POST)
messages.note: Source IP address identifies the Device.

messages.label: error (200 OK)
messages.note: Instead of a locationResponse, if no location can be given.

viz.caption: THE EIGHT INITIAL HELD ERROR CODES (RFC 5985)

items.label: Bad request
items.desc: The request was badly formed, other than its XML content.

items.label: Bad XML
items.desc: The XML content was badly formed or invalid.

items.label: LIS failure
items.desc: An unspecified error occurred at the LIS.

items.label: Location unknown
items.desc: The LIS could not determine the location; retry later but limit attempts.

items.label: Unsupported element
items.desc: A document element in the request was not supported.

items.label: Timed out
items.desc: The LIS could not answer within the responseTime.

items.label: Type unavailable
items.desc: The requested location type is unavailable and exact was true.

items.label: Not locatable
items.desc: The Device is outside the LIS network; it MUST NOT try again.
